claim: Neurite outgrowth is driven in part by microtubule-sliding – the transport of microtubules along each other.
source: Neurite outgrowth is driven in part by microtubule-sliding – the transport of microtubules along each other.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: A 'mitotic' kinesin-6 (Pavarotti in Drosophila) effectively inhibits microtubule-sliding and neurite outgrowth.
source: We have recently demonstrated that a 'mitotic' kinesin-6 (Pavarotti in Drosophila) effectively inhibits microtubule-sliding and neurite outgrowth.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous work from the authors' group as referenced in the abstract and introduction.

claim: The inhibition of microtubule-sliding by Pavarotti is controlled by phosphorylation.
source: the inhibition of microtubule-sliding by Pavarotti is controlled by phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through multiple experiments including sliding assays with phospho-null mutants and phospho-specific antibodies.

claim: The Ser/Thr NDR kinase Tricornered (Trc) is a Pavarotti-dependent regulator of microtubule sliding in neurons.
source: We identify the Ser/Thr NDR kinase Tricornered (Trc) as a Pavarotti-dependent regulator of microtubule sliding in neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated through RNAi experiments showing Trc depletion increases sliding, and that this effect requires Pavarotti.

claim: Trc-mediated phosphorylation of Pavarotti promotes its interaction with 14-3-3 proteins.
source: we show that Trc-mediated phosphorylation of Pavarotti promotes its interaction with 14-3-3 proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing increased Pavarotti-14-3-3 interaction with Trc overexpression and loss of interaction with S745A mutation.

claim: Loss of 14-3-3 prevents Pavarotti from associating with microtubules.
source: Loss of 14-3-3 prevents Pavarotti from associating with microtubules.
evidence: This is shown through extraction experiments measuring microtubule-associated Pavarotti upon 14-3-3 depletion.

claim: Depletion of Trc by dsRNA leads to a significant increase in microtubule sliding in S2 cells compared to control.
source: We found a significant increase in microtubule sliding upon depletion of Trc compared to control (Figure 1A, quantified in B, Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through photoconversion experiments measuring microtubule sliding rates, with quantification shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Neurons are exceptionally dependent on microtubules for long-range transport of cargo.
source: Neurons are exceptionally dependent on microtubules for long-range transport of cargo.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Microtubule organization is essential for powering initial neurite outgrowth (Kapitein and Hoogenraad, 2015; Lu et al., 2013; Winding et al., 2016).
source: microtubule organization is essential for powering initial neurite outgrowth (Kapitein and Hoogenraad, 2015; Lu et al., 2013; Winding et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In cultured Drosophila neurons, microtubules can be seen pushing the plasma membrane at the tips of growing processes (del Castillo et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2013).
source: Indeed, in cultured Drosophila neurons, microtubules can be seen pushing the plasma membrane at the tips of growing processes (del Castillo et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work from the authors' group.

claim: Kinesin-1 is the motor responsible for the majority of microtubule sliding in neurons (Lu et al., 2013; Winding et al., 2016).
source: Previous work from our group has identified the classical kinesin – Kinesin-1 – as the motor responsible for the majority of microtubule sliding in neurons (Lu et al., 2013; Winding et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work from the authors' group.

claim: Microtubule sliding is observed in young neurons in culture, but decreases as neurons mature (Lu et al., 2013).
source: Microtubule sliding is observed in young neurons in culture, but decreases as neurons mature (Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Depletion of Pavarotti/MKLP1 by RNAi leads to axon hyperextension and more motile microtubules (Del Castillo et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2012).
source: Depletion of Pavarotti/MKLP1 by RNAi leads to axon hyperextension and more motile microtubules (Del Castillo et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Kinesin-6 exists as a heterotetramer with MgcRacGAP (Tumbleweed in Drosophila) to form the centralspindlin complex (Adams et al., 1998; Basant and Glotzer, 2018; Mishima et al., 2002).
source: It exists as a heterotetramer with MgcRacGAP (Tumbleweed in Drosophila) to form the centralspindlin complex (Adams et al., 1998; Basant and Glotzer, 2018; Mishima et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The centralspindlin complex bundles microtubules at the bipolar spindle in late anaphase (Hutterer et al., 2009).
source: This complex bundles microtubules at the bipolar spindle in late anaphase (Hutterer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The centralspindlin complex can locally activate RhoA and promote assembly of the contractile actin ring at the cortex, and so, cytokinesis (Basant and Glotzer, 2018; Verma and Maresca, 2019).
source: Here, it can locally activate RhoA and promote assembly of the contractile actin ring at the cortex, and so, cytokinesis (Basant and Glotzer, 2018; Verma and Maresca, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylation is a well-studied facet of centralspindlin regulation in regards to mitotic progression (Douglas et al., 2010; Guse et al., 2005).
source: One well-studied facet of centralspindlin regulation in regards to mitotic progression is that of phosphorylation (Douglas et al., 2010; Guse et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The NDR kinase Tricornered (Trc, LATS in mammals) has been shown to phosphorylate MKLP1, the human ortholog of Pavarotti, in vitro at S710 (S745 in Pavarotti) (Okamoto et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
source: One potential kinase was the NDR kinase Tricornered (Trc, LATS in mammals) – shown to phosphorylate MKLP1, the human ortholog of Pavarotti, in vitro at S710 (S745 in Pavarotti) (Okamoto et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and reference to a figure showing the phosphorylation site.

claim: Trc regulates cell cycle exit (Hergovich et al., 2006).
source: Trc regulates cell cycle exit (Hergovich et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Trc regulates microtubule sliding and dendrite outgrowth in neurons.
source: we use Drosophila S2 cells, neuronal culture and in vivo imaging to show Trc regulates microtubule sliding and dendrite outgrowth in neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through multiple experimental approaches including S2 cell assays, neuronal cultures, and in vivo imaging.

claim: Pavarotti is a Trc substrate.
source: We validate Pavarotti as a Trc substrate
evidence: This is demonstrated through phospho-specific antibody experiments and co-expression studies.

claim: Phosphorylation of Pavarotti affects its subcellular distribution via interaction with 14-3-3 proteins in interphase cells.
source: We also show that phosphorylation of Pavarotti affects its subcellular distribution via interaction with 14-3-3 proteins in interphase cells
evidence: This is demonstrated through extraction experiments and co-immunoprecipitation studies.

claim: The mechanism of Pavarotti regulation via 14-3-3 interaction is conserved from mitosis.
source: phosphorylation of Pavarotti affects its subcellular distribution via interaction with 14-3-3 proteins in interphase cells – a mechanism conserved from mitosis.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with mitotic mechanisms and supported by citations.

claim: Pavarotti inhibits microtubule sliding in S2 cells (Del Castillo et al., 2015; Jolly et al., 2010).
source: We have previously demonstrated that kinesin-1 carries out microtubule-microtubule sliding in these cells and that Pavarotti inhibits this (Del Castillo et al., 2015; Jolly et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work from the authors' group.

claim: Depletion of Trc with dsRNA against a non-coding region increases microtubule sliding in S2 cells, and expression of wild-type Trc rescues this effect.
source: To do this, we decreased Trc levels with dsRNA against a non-coding region of Trc, and co-expressed wild-type Trc. The non-coding dsRNA increased microtubule sliding and expression of wild-type Trc rescued this effect.
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments with rescue constructs as shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The effect of Trc depletion on microtubule sliding is specific to Trc depletion and not an off-target effect.
source: Therefore, the effect is specific to Trc depletion (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through rescue experiments showing specificity.

claim: Trc depletion leads to a dramatic increase in total neurite length per cell in vitro in primary neuronal cultures from third instar larvae.
source: We found a dramatic increase in total neurite length per cell in vitro (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through measurements of cultured neurons with quantification shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Depleting Trc levels leads to an increase in microtubule sliding rate in cultured primary neurons.
source: Consistent with our data in S2 cells, we found that depleting Trc levels led to an increase in microtubule sliding rate in cultured primary neurons (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through photoconversion experiments in neurons with quantification shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Trc has the ability to modulate microtubule sliding in order to control neurite outgrowth.
source: Therefore, Trc has the ability to modulate microtubule sliding in order to control neurite outgrowth.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing Trc regulates both sliding and neurite length.

claim: Trc regulates neurite outgrowth independent from cell division.
source: These data describe a role for Trc as a negative regulator of neuronal development, independent from cell division
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that effects are seen in post-mitotic neurons.

claim: The mechanism by which Trc regulates neurite outgrowth is via microtubule sliding.
source: suggest that the mechanism by which Trc regulates neurite outgrowth is via microtubule sliding.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between Trc's effects on sliding and neurite length.

claim: The effect of Trc on sliding could likely be intrinsic, rather than dependent on external cues, as the effect can be seen in dissociated cultures.
source: This effect could likely be intrinsic, rather than dependent on external cues, as the effect can be seen in dissociated cultures.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that effects persist in dissociated culture conditions.

claim: Wild-type and constitutively active Trc are able to reduce microtubule sliding to similar levels as control samples, but kinase-dead Trc is not.
source: We found that while WT and constitutively active Trc were able to reduce microtubule sliding to similar levels as control samples, the kinase dead mutant was not.
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments with different Trc mutants as shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Furry (Fry) is a large protein shown to promote Trc kinase activity without affecting expression level (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Emoto et al., 2006).
source: Furry is a large protein shown to promote Trc kinase activity without affecting expression level (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Emoto et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to a figure showing protein levels.

claim: Knockdown of Fry leads to an increase in microtubule sliding in S2 cells.
source: Upon knockdown of Fry, and so decrease in Trc kinase activity, we found an increase in microtubule sliding (Figure 2C,D Video 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments with Fry depletion as shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Depleting Fry, and so decreasing Trc kinase activity, leads to an increase in microtubule sliding in neurons.
source: We found that depleting Fry, and so decreasing Trc kinase activity, led to an increase in microtubule sliding (Figure 2E,F Video 5)
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments in neurons with Fry depletion as shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: The kinase activity of Trc is required to regulate microtubule sliding.
source: these experiments show that the kinase activity of Trc is required to regulate microtubule sliding
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with kinase-dead mutants and Fry depletion.

claim: The findings regarding Trc regulation of microtubule sliding are consistent between Drosophila neurons and S2 cells.
source: these findings are consistent between Drosophila neurons and S2 cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar results obtained in both cell types.

claim: Overexpression of Trc in S2 cells results in a decrease in microtubule sliding.
source: Overexpression of Trc in S2 cells resulted in a decrease in microtubule sliding.
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments with Trc overexpression as shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Upon depletion of Pavarotti, the decrease in sliding caused by Trc overexpression is lost.
source: Importantly, upon depletion of Pavarotti, this decrease in sliding was lost (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments combining Trc overexpression and Pavarotti depletion as shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Pavarotti must be present for Trc to oppose microtubule-microtubule sliding.
source: Therefore, Pavarotti must be present for Trc to oppose microtubule-microtubule sliding.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Trc overexpression cannot decrease sliding when Pavarotti is depleted.

claim: Pavarotti is phosphorylated by Trc at Ser 745 in cells.
source: Therefore, Trc phosphorylates Pavarotti at Ser 745 in cells (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is demonstrated through western blot analysis with phospho-specific antibody showing increased phosphorylation with Trc overexpression as shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Ectopic expression of constitutively active Trc (Trc CA) results in a roughly twofold increase in Pavarotti phosphorylated at S745.
source: Importantly, ectopic expression of constitutively active Trc (Trc CA), resulted in a roughly twofold increase in Pavarotti phosphorylated at S745.
evidence: This is demonstrated through western blot analysis as shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Trc phosphorylates Pavarotti at serine 745 in neurons in vivo.
source: Therefore, Trc phosphorylates Pavarotti at serine 745 in neurons in vivo
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunoprecipitation from brain tissue and western blot analysis as shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Depletion of Trc leads to a greater pool of unphosphorylated Pavarotti at S745.
source: depletion of the kinase leads to a greater pool of unphosphorylated Pavarotti at S745.
evidence: This is demonstrated through western blot analysis showing reduced phospho-Pavarotti upon Trc depletion as shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Phospho-Pavarotti is reduced by around 35% upon Trc depletion when compared to total immunoprecipitated Pavarotti.
source: We found that phospho Pavarotti was reduced by around 35% upon Trc depletion when compared to total immunoprecipitated Pavarotti.
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantification of western blot data from brain tissue.

claim: Depletion of Pavarotti with a dsRNA against a non-coding region increases sliding which can be reduced again by expression of wild-type Pavarotti.
source: Depletion of Pavarotti with a dsRNA against a non-coding region increased sliding which could be reduced again by expression of wild-type Pavarotti.
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments with knockdown and rescue as shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Expression of Pavarotti S745A mutant fails to reduce sliding levels to their control levels.
source: However, expression of Pavarotti S745A mutant failed to reduce sliding levels to their control levels (Figure 3C,D, Video 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments with phospho-null mutant as shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Pavarotti can no longer inhibit microtubule sliding when phosphorylation of S745 is prevented.
source: Therefore, Pavarotti can no longer inhibit microtubule sliding when phosphorylation of S745 is prevented.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that S745A mutant cannot rescue the sliding phenotype.

claim: Depletion of Trc leads to around a 50% decrease in association of Pavarotti with microtubules.
source: We found that depletion of Trc led to around a 50% decrease in association of Pavarotti with microtubules (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through extraction experiments measuring microtubule-associated Pavarotti as shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The phospho-null mutant S745A shows a decrease in association of Pavarotti with microtubules.
source: Similar experiments with the phospho-null mutant S745A also show a decrease in association of Pavarotti with microtubules (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through extraction experiments as shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: Pavarotti in its unphosphorylated state has lower affinity for microtubules.
source: Therefore, Pavarotti in its unphosphorylated state has lower affinity for microtubules.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Trc depletion and S745A mutation both decrease Pavarotti-microtubule association.

claim: Under conditions where Pavarotti is unphosphorylated, microtubule sliding is permitted.
source: Under these conditions, microtubule sliding is permitted.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between decreased Pavarotti-microtubule association and increased sliding.

claim: 14-3-3 proteins have been shown to form a complex with Pavarotti dependent upon phosphorylation at the identified S745 site (Douglas et al., 2010; Fesquet et al., 2015).
source: These proteins have been shown to form a complex with Pavarotti dependent upon phosphorylation at the identified S745 site (Douglas et al., 2010; Fesquet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The association between Pavarotti and 14-3-3 influences microtubule bundling (Douglas et al., 2010).
source: This association influences microtubule bundling (Douglas et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: There is a robust interaction between WT Pavarotti and endogenous 14-3-3 ξ.
source: We found a robust interaction between WT Pavarotti and endogenous 14-3-3 ξ.
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mutation of S745 to alanine, mimicking a non-phosphorylated form of Pavarotti, abrogates the interaction with 14-3-3.
source: Mutation of S745 to alanine, mimicking a non-phosphorylated form of Pavarotti, abrogated the interaction.
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Co-expression of exogenous Trc with GFP Pavarotti increases the interaction between Pavarotti and 14-3-3 ξ by roughly 60%.
source: Co-expression of exogenous Trc with GFP Pavarotti, generating a greater pool of phosphorylated Pavarotti at S745, increases the interaction between Pavarotti and 14-3-3 ξ by roughly 60% (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation experiments as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Phosphorylation of Pavarotti, by Trc, leads to the recruitment of 14-3-3 proteins.
source: Therefore, we confirm that phosphorylation of Pavarotti, by Trc, leads to the recruitment of 14-3-3 proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data showing Trc-dependent interaction.

claim: Overexpression of Pavarotti causes a decrease in microtubule sliding.
source: Overexpression of Pavarotti caused a decrease in microtubule sliding.
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments as shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: When 14-3-3 levels are depleted, the decrease in sliding upon Pavarotti overexpression is no longer observed.
source: However, when we depleted 14-3-3 levels, we no longer observed this decrease in sliding upon Pavarotti overexpression (Figure 4B, quantified in C, Video 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments combining Pavarotti overexpression and 14-3-3 depletion as shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Pavarotti is not capable of inhibiting microtubule sliding in the absence of 14-3-3 proteins.
source: Thus, Pavarotti is not capable of inhibiting microtubule sliding in the absence of 14-3-3 proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Pavarotti overexpression cannot decrease sliding when 14-3-3 is depleted.

claim: Depletion of 14-3-3 shows a decrease in GFP Pavarotti associated with microtubules.
source: Observation of the microtubule network in this condition showed a decrease in GFP Pavarotti associated with microtubules (Figure 4D,E
evidence: This is demonstrated through extraction experiments as shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: Pavarotti locally brakes microtubule sliding and this is facilitated by interaction with 14-3-3 proteins.
source: our data suggest Pavarotti locally brakes microtubule sliding and this is facilitated by interaction with 14-3-3 proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing 14-3-3 is required for Pavarotti to inhibit sliding and associate with microtubules.

claim: The formation of the Pavarotti-14-3-3 complex requires phosphorylation at S745, by the kinase Trc.
source: The formation of this complex requires phosphorylation at S745, by the kinase Trc.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing Trc phosphorylates S745 and this phosphorylation is required for 14-3-3 interaction.

claim: Depleting Pavarotti leads to a roughly twofold increase in microtubule sliding rate in neurons.
source: We found that, like Trc, depleting Pavarotti led to a roughly twofold increase in microtubule sliding rate in neurons (Figure 5A quantified in B, Video 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments in neurons as shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Pavarotti regulates dendrite development in Drosophila.
source: Notably, this is the first report of Pavarotti regulating dendrite development in Drosophila.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding based on the in vivo dendrite measurements.

claim: Pavarotti prevents axon overgrowth (Del Castillo et al., 2015).
source: Previous work has shown Pavarotti prevents axon overgrowth (Del Castillo et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Reports in mammalian systems have suggested roles for Pavarotti in both axons and dendrites (Lin et al., 2012).
source: reports in mammalian systems have suggested roles in both compartments (Lin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Knockdown of both Pavarotti and Trc together increases microtubule sliding to similar levels to those of either knockdown individually.
source: Importantly, knockdown of both Pavarotti and Trc together increased microtubule sliding to similar levels to those of either knockdown individually – double knockdown had no additive effect.
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments with double knockdown as shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Pavarotti and Trc regulate microtubule sliding in neurons via the same pathway.
source: This supports the hypothesis that Pavarotti and Trc regulate microtubule sliding in neurons via the same pathway
evidence: This is inferred from the non-additive effect of double knockdown.

claim: Depletion of either Trc or Pavarotti leads to increased dendrite length in class IV DA neurons.
source: In each case, we observed a roughly 40% increase in total dendrite length (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vivo measurements of dendrite length as shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Depletion of both Trc and Pavarotti simultaneously has no additive effect on dendrite outgrowth.
source: Notably, the effect upon double knockdown was equivalent to that of the single knockdowns (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vivo measurements as shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Trc and Pavarotti act in a common pathway to regulate neurite outgrowth.
source: This supports the hypothesis that Trc and Pavarotti regulate neurite outgrowth in concert.
evidence: This is inferred from the non-additive effect of double knockdown on dendrite length.

claim: Trc has been previously shown to increase dendrite branching (Emoto et al., 2004).
source: Trc has been previously shown to increase dendrite branching (Emoto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Trc RNAi cells have roughly 30% more branch points than controls.
source: Our analyses reproduced these findings – Trc RNAi cells had roughly 30% more branch points than controls.
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantification of branch points as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pavarotti depletion has no effect on number of branch points.
source: Interestingly, Pavarotti depletion had no effect on number of branch points
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantification of branch points as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Depletion of Trc and Pavarotti together mimics the effect of Trc RNAi alone on branch points.
source: depletion of Trc and Pavarotti together mimics the effect of Trc RNAi alone.
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantification of branch points as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Trc and Pavarotti regulate neurite outgrowth together, but Trc has another role, independent of Pavarotti phosphorylation, in regulating dendritic branching.
source: From these data, we infer that Trc and Pavarotti regulate neurite outgrowth together, but that Trc has another role, independent of Pavarotti phosphorylation, in regulating dendritic branching.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on branching versus length.

claim: Trc regulates microtubule sliding in neurons together with Pavarotti.
source: our data demonstrate that Trc regulates microtubule sliding in neurons together with Pavarotti
evidence: This is demonstrated through multiple experiments showing non-additive effects of double knockdown.

claim: Trc phosphorylates Pavarotti at S745.
source: this kinase phosphorylates Pavarotti at S745.
evidence: This is demonstrated through phospho-specific antibody experiments.

claim: Pavarotti phosphorylation at S745 is required to brake microtubule sliding and correctly tailor neurite extension.
source: Pavarotti phosphorylation at S745 is required to brake microtubule sliding and so, correctly tailor neurite extension.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing S745 phosphorylation is required for sliding inhibition and proper neurite development.

claim: Microtubule sliding is diminished in mature neurons by the action of Drosophila kinesin-6, Pavarotti.
source: microtubule-microtubule sliding is required for neurite outgrowth in young neurons and is diminished in mature neurons by the action of Drosophila kinesin-6, Pavarotti.
evidence: This is supported by previous work from the authors' group.

claim: The yeast homologue of Trc (Dbf2p) promotes chromosome segregation and mitotic exit.
source: The yeast homologue of Trc (Dbf2p) promotes chromosome segregation and mitotic exit.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The functions of Trc in chromosome segregation and mitotic exit are conserved in mammals (Hergovich et al., 2006; Tamaskovic et al., 2003).
source: These functions are conserved in mammals (Hergovich et al., 2006; Tamaskovic et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Neuronal expression of some NDR kinases has been reported.
source: However, neuronal expression of some NDR kinases has additionally been reported.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Depletion of Trc has been linked to increased outgrowth of both axons and dendrites across multiple taxa (Emoto et al., 2004; Gallegos and Bargmann, 2004; Ultanir et al., 2012; Zallen et al., 1999).
source: In neurons, depletion of Trc has been linked to increased outgrowth of both axons and dendrites across multiple taxa (Emoto et al., 2004; Gallegos and Bargmann, 2004; Ultanir et al., 2012; Zallen et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The data are in good agreement with previous reports showing Trc depletion increases neurite length.
source: Our data are in good agreement with these previous reports as we measure an increase in neurite length in vitro and an increase in dendrite length in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with previous literature.

claim: Expression of a sliding deficient kinesin-1 mutant drastically decreases the dendritic arbors of Drosophila sensory neurons (Class IV DA neurons) (Winding et al., 2016).
source: Indeed, this sliding has been shown to translate into dendrite outgrowth in vivo – expression of a sliding deficient kinesin-1 mutant drastically decreases the dendritic arbors of Drosophila sensory neurons (Class IV DA neurons) (Winding et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Pavarotti is a microtubule cross linker and signaling hub to promote cleavage furrow ingress (Adams et al., 1998; Basant and Glotzer, 2017; Verma and Maresca, 2019).
source: It is a microtubule cross linker and signaling hub to promote cleavage furrow ingress (Adams et al., 1998; Basant and Glotzer, 2017; Verma and Maresca, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Pavarotti's ability to localize to the spindle is dependent on its phosphorylation state (Guse et al., 2005).
source: Moreover, Pavarotti's ability to localize to the spindle is dependent on its phosphorylation state (Guse et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Pavarotti is a downstream effector of Trc in the sliding inhibition pathway.
source: we have shown that Pavarotti is a downstream effector of Trc in the sliding inhibition pathway
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments showing Trc requires Pavarotti to inhibit sliding.

claim: Trc overexpression could only decrease sliding in the presence of Pavarotti.
source: Trc overexpression could only decrease sliding in the presence of Pavarotti.
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments as shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: In neurons, depletion of both Pavarotti and Trc together had the same effect as depletion of either protein individually.
source: In agreement with these data, in neurons, depletion of both Pavarotti and Trc together had the same effect as depletion of either protein individually.
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding and dendrite measurements as shown in Figure 5.

claim: Wild type and constitutively active Trc constructs could restore normal sliding levels but a kinase dead variant was unable to do this.
source: Knockdown and rescue experiments in S2 cells showed wild type and constitutively active Trc constructs could restore normal sliding levels but, a kinase dead variant was unable to do this.
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments as shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Decrease of Fry protein level increases microtubule sliding.
source: This is supported by data in neurons showing that decrease of Fry protein level increases microtubule sliding.
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments as shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Decreasing Fry decreases Trc kinase activity without affecting protein level (Emoto et al., 2004).
source: Decreasing Fry decreases Trc kinase activity without affecting protein level (Emoto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylation of Pavarotti at the proposed Trc site of Serine 745 is necessary to inhibit sliding.
source: we have used a phospho-null mutant to demonstrate that phosphorylation of Pavarotti at the proposed Trc site of Serine 745 is necessary to inhibit sliding.
evidence: This is demonstrated through sliding experiments with S745A mutant as shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Drosophila Pavarotti is phosphorylated at S745 by Trc in neurons.
source: we confirm biochemically that Drosophila Pavarotti is phosphorylated at this site by Trc in neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated through western blot analysis of brain tissue as shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The pathway of Trc phosphorylating Pavarotti at S745 is conserved between humans and Drosophila (Fesquet et al., 2015).
source: This extends previous reports to show this pathway is conserved between humans and Drosophila (Fesquet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with previous work and supported by citation.

claim: The in vitro data suggest that Trc and Pavarotti act together to regulate sliding in developing cultured neurons.
source: Our in vitro data suggest that these two proteins act together to regulate sliding in developing cultured neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data in cultured neurons.

claim: In vivo, Trc and Pavarotti work in concert to regulate neuronal development.
source: In vivo, we demonstrate that these two proteins work in concert to regulate neuronal development.
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vivo dendrite measurements.

claim: Toll-6-FoxO mutants have increased microtubule stability (McLaughlin et al., 2016).
source: Toll-6-FoxO mutants have increased microtubule stability (McLaughlin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Phosphorylation would provide a more dynamic method for modulating Pavarotti than protein translation.
source: However, phosphorylation would provide more dynamic method for modulating Pavarotti.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the advantages of phosphorylation-based regulation.

claim: Phosphorylation would provide tighter spatial regulation which could be necessary in inhibiting sliding in primary neurites while secondary processes are still developing.
source: Moreover, phosphorylation would provide tighter spatial regulation which could be necessary in inhibiting sliding in primary neurites while secondary processes are still developing.
